newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Thais almost done on corn imports, eyes on weather.
newsitem.headline: Thais almost done on corn imports, eyes on weather.

text.p: Thailand is said to have virtually completed buying 150,000 tonnes of tariff-free corn while concern in the trade about the impact of dry weather on crops around the region increased, traders said on Thursday.

The Thai government on Tuesday approved a request by local feedmills to import the grain because of a shortage stemming from a dry spell in the country. Bangkok had earlier estimated the shortage at between 175,000-200,000 tonnes.
"A lot of the Thai feedmills bought before the order was even issued," a dealer said.
"Most of the 150,000 tonnes should be covered by now," another dealer said, adding the Thais would probably only need to buy some 20,000 tonnes of corn to round out their purchases.
But one senior dealer felt the Thais may have only locked up 100,000 tonnes of corn.
"I believe there's still 50,000 tonnes of corn to go in Thailand," he said.
The Thais were buying corn in transit and most dealers believe the likely origin will be the U.S. as Bangkok does not usually import Chinese corn.
With Malaysia having ample supplies, the trade is keeping an eye on Indonesia as a drought hammers the October/November corn crop in East Java, dealers said.
Indonesia would need at least 200,000 tonnes of corn by year-end if the crop suffers badly from the dry spell, which has been linked to the El Nino weather phenomenon.
Jakarta has already bought 150,000 tonnes of mainly Chinese corn and the grain is scheduled to arrive by mid-August.

"The Indonesians will have to make a decision by late-August because they're looking at September/October corn shipments. They're hoping some rain will fall in the U.S. Midwest and soften (futures) prices in Chicago," a dealer said.
Corn prices in the U.S. have firmed recently due to concerns about dry weather in the Midwest corn belt of the country, especially in Illinois and the western part of Indiana.
The dry conditions around Southeast Asia and in the U.S. caused jitters among buyers worried about spikes in grain prices on the Chicago Board of Trade (CBOT).

Traders placed most of the blame for the dry spell in Asia on El Nino, a warming of the Pacific Ocean off South America which disrupts global weather patterns and often brings drought to Asia-Pacific countries and rampant floods elsewhere.
"It looks like this is the El Nino and there is some concern whether that is also happenning in China," a dealer said.

Drought in three major corn producing provinces in China may knock Beijing out of the corn market and eliminate an alternate source of supply for buyers in the region, particularly Indonesia and Malaysia.

"I don't see the Chinese exporting corn this year," one grains analyst said. "If they see a tight situation developing, they'll shut off the corn exports. But I don't think the problem is bad enough there that they will import corn. They just won't export any."

Soymeal demand in Southeast Asia, on the other hand, remains strong and Indonesia, Malaysia and Thailand would need to buy a combined 100,000 tonnes of meal from October onwards for their rapidly expanding poultry and livestock industry, dealers said.
